top_choice_rationale: P002 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) with a citation confined to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification rewards a settled conceptual result: the invariant and protected helical edge states were predicted and then unambiguously observed in HgTe, and fifteen to twenty years of transport, spectroscopy and first-principles work have left the interpretation stable and made the invariant a routine materials-design criterion. The 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and Hall plateaux with broken time-reversal symmetry, so this is a distinct statement. The credit gap (the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, Zhang deceased, plus the 3D and QAH strands) is real and should be stated openly rather than hidden, but it is comparable in size to the credit tail of P001, whose clean Katori-Ye pairing and realised uses make it a close and defensible second. P003 is a striking prediction-then-experiment pair but is early, with the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder unsettled and key experimentalists outside the three names; no award is least preferred because at least two proposals are mature and prize-worthy.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my electronic-structure and magnetism research in Uppsala materials theory is adjacent to the topological-materials theme of P002, which I disclose as possible bias, but I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer
